cards.claim: The candidate chose not to build the obvious thing — a tool that scores candidates — and instead focused on a harder real problem: helping reviewers read very different submissions fairly and consistently.

citation.quote:
The obvious build is a candidate-scoring screener. I built the
opposite, on purpose.

By keeping the format open to be fair across eight backgrounds, the brief
guarantees the panel an apples-to-oranges problem at volume

refutation.rationale: The README plainly says 'The obvious build is a candidate-scoring screener. I built the opposite, on purpose' and explains the reasoning around reviewer consistency with different submission formats. The quote directly supports the claim.

cards.claim: The candidate named a specific reason the original signal is getting weaker — AI-polished submissions — and argued the real value is in surfacing citable evidence and generating interview questions.

citation.quote:
applicants now use AI to
produce polished artifacts at machine speed, so the artifact alone is a
weakening signal. What holds up is evidence you can cite, doubts you can name,
and questions a candidate who did the work can answer easily

refutation.rationale: The quoted passage from the README explicitly names AI-polished submissions as a weakening signal and argues the real value is in citable evidence and interview questions. The claim accurately reflects what is written.

cards.claim: The candidate defined five specific criteria for what 'evaluate well' means, going beyond the vague brief and committing to a concrete direction with stated reasons.

citation.quote:
The brief leaves "evaluate an AI Builder well" open, so this is my definition,
and the system is built to it:

1. **Evidence over impressions.** Every claim about a candidate must be
   traceable to something the candidate actually submitted

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md lists five numbered criteria under 'What evaluate well means here,' starting with 'Evidence over impressions.' The quote is the opening of that list and the claim accurately describes it.

cards.claim: The candidate tied the score-free design to a real governance constraint — citing a named policy from the hiring organisation — making it a reasoned constraint, not a preference.

citation.quote:
KPMG's own recruiting communications state it plainly: "no hiring
   decisions are made using AI… We believe technology should empower human
   judgment, not replace it." A scoring screener would contradict the
   policy of the organization it's built for

refutation.rationale: The DECISIONS.md quote directly attributes the no-scoring position to KPMG's own stated policy, naming it as a governance constraint rather than a personal preference. The claim accurately represents this.

cards.claim: The submission includes a five-stage pipeline table that names each stage, who acts, what level of control they have, what they produce, and where a human must step in.

citation.quote:
| Stage | Actor | Autonomy | Output | Human gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S0 intake + redaction | Deterministic code | Full | Normalized text + escrowed redaction map | None needed — no model judgment |

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table in the README has all five columns — Stage, Actor, Autonomy, Output, Human gate — and the quoted row is one of five rows shown. The table is present and matches the claim.

cards.claim: The probe sheet is hard-locked until a human has reviewed every evidence card, which is a concrete technical gate that forces human judgment before the AI's summary is visible.

citation.quote: **Hard-locked** until a human dispositions every card

refutation.rationale: The README pipeline table shows 'Hard-locked until a human dispositions every card' in the Human gate column for the S3 probes + synthesis stage. The claim accurately describes this.

cards.claim: Each pipeline stage has a named, justified level of AI control: 'create-only', 'annotate-only', or 'constrained' — and the candidate explains why each level was chosen.

citation.quote: S1 evidence extraction | Claude (charitable reader) | **Create-only** | Evidence cards: claim, competency, verbatim citation, substance grade | Every card born `unconfirmed`

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table does show three named autonomy levels (Create-only, Annotate-only, Constrained), but the submission only briefly notes what each means in the table itself. A fuller explanation of why each level was chosen is not clearly present in the documents — only the labels and a short description in the table.

cards.claim: The skeptic stage is explicitly designed never to auto-resolve disagreements — it can only annotate, and all conflicts are surfaced to a human reviewer.

citation.quote: S2 adversarial refutation | Claude (independent skeptic) | **Annotate-only** | `supported` / `unverified` / `contradicted` + counter-citation | Disagreements surfaced, never auto-resolved

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table entry for S2 reads 'Annotate-only' and 'Disagreements surfaced, never auto-resolved,' which directly supports both parts of this claim.

cards.claim: A live demo is publicly available with no setup or API key required, running on pre-computed pipeline outputs.

citation.quote:
**Live demo:** [second-reader.vercel.app](https://second-reader.vercel.app) —
no setup, no API key needed. The demo runs on precomputed pipeline outputs,
disclosed on screen as demo mode; the "Re-run pipeline (live)" button runs the
real thing.

refutation.rationale: The README states the live demo URL, says no setup or API key is needed, and discloses that it runs on precomputed pipeline outputs. The claim accurately reflects what is written.

cards.claim: The tool enforces its no-score rule in code via schema validation — there are no score fields in the data types, not just a prompt instruction telling the model not to score.

citation.quote:
**No score fields exist.** Not "the model is told not to score" — the zod
  schemas at every model boundary have nowhere to put one
  ([lib/types.ts](lib/types.ts), [lib/pipeline/schemas.ts](lib/pipeline/schemas.ts)).

refutation.rationale: The README says 'the zod schemas at every model boundary have nowhere to put one' and cites two specific files. The claim that this is enforced in code rather than via a prompt instruction is directly backed by the quote.

cards.claim: The rubric is a swappable config file, and the candidate explains the same pipeline pattern can be reused for vendor proposals, QA, or policy review by changing only that file.

citation.quote:
Swap [rubric/rubric.json](rubric/rubric.json) and nothing else: the same
cited-evidence, adversarially-checked, human-gated review pattern reads vendor
proposals against procurement criteria, engagement deliverables against QA
standards, or policy documents against control frameworks.

refutation.rationale: The README's Reuse section says to swap the rubric file 'and nothing else' and lists three concrete reuse scenarios. The claim accurately describes this as a described (not demonstrated) capability.

cards.claim: The project has an automated eval suite that runs in CI and fails the build if any guarantee is violated, covering citation accuracy, injection resistance, and recall against hand-labelled test cases.

citation.quote:
`npm run eval` checks citation
  fidelity (zero tolerance), injection resistance, detection of a planted
  cross-document contradiction, the vocabulary ban, and recall/precision
  against hand-labeled golden cases — and CI fails if a committed run violates
  a guarantee.

refutation.rationale: The README describes the eval suite and says CI fails on violations, but the actual eval report (evals/report.md) and CI configuration are not in the submitted documents, so the claim that CI actually fails cannot be confirmed from the text alone. The claim is graded 'demonstrated' but the evidence is a description, not an observable output.

cards.claim: The candidate describes a real failure in the eval suite itself — the injection-resistance check was passing incorrectly — and explains exactly how they fixed it twice.

citation.quote:
The injection-resistance check FAILED on a run where the pipeline had behaved
correctly: it flagged candidate B's planted injection and the synthesis
reported it to the panel as a finding… My check just pattern-matched
the injection's words anywhere in the synthesis, so it couldn't tell
*describing the attack* from *obeying it*.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md describes the injection-resistance check failing, explains the two-step fix in detail, and names the root cause each time. The claim accurately represents this account.

cards.claim: The candidate reports specific precision numbers from real runs and explains exactly which cards were invalid and why — including that all invalid cards were either machine-flagged or skeptic-contested before a human saw them.

citation.quote:
16/20 cards on candidate A and 12/13 on
candidate B hand-labelled valid. The invalids are the four citation
mis-quotes above, plus one card on A that graded a "the demo video shows it
running" transcript claim as `demonstrated`

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md gives specific card counts (16/20 and 12/13) and identifies exactly which cards were invalid and why. The claim's key point — that all invalid cards were machine-flagged or skeptic-contested before human review — is stated explicitly: 'every invalid card was either machine-flagged or skeptic-contested before any human looked.'

cards.claim: The candidate changed how recall was measured after finding the original metric was unstable — it was too strict about which competency a piece of evidence was filed under — and explains why the new definition is more honest.

citation.quote:
An early version checked that each expected finding was extracted *under a specific skill*. But the model legitimately files the same evidence under different defensible skills across runs… So recall
now asks only "was this evidence surfaced at all?" — which is the honest
definition and stops the metric thrashing on re-runs.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md explains the original recall metric checked for evidence filed under a specific competency, why that caused instability, and how the new definition (was the evidence surfaced at all?) is more honest. The claim accurately represents this.

cards.claim: Submissions addressed to AI systems are automatically extracted as flagged findings, and the system is tested against a planted injection in one of the demo submissions.

citation.quote:
**Submissions are data, not instructions.** Text addressed to AI systems is
  extracted as a flagged finding. Candidate B's pitch contains a planted
  injection; watch what the pipeline does with it.

refutation.rationale: The README explicitly states that text addressed to AI systems is extracted as a flagged finding, and names candidate B's planted injection as a test case. Both parts of the claim are directly supported.

cards.claim: The transparency page is generated from the same rubric file the pipeline actually uses, so the public disclosure of how the system works cannot drift out of date.

citation.quote:
The
  [transparency page](app/transparency/page.tsx) is rendered from the same
  rubric file the pipeline runs on, so the disclosure cannot drift from the
  system it describes.

refutation.rationale: The README states that the transparency page is rendered from the same rubric file the pipeline uses, so the two cannot drift apart. The claim accurately reflects this.

cards.claim: The candidate names a concrete risk — that prose style can still reveal demographic information even after redaction — and is honest that the fix (an AI redaction pass) was not shipped because it wasn't tested.

citation.quote: Regex-only redaction (S0) | Prose style, school names in sentences, project choices can still proxy for demographics | An LLM redaction pass is an API call away, but testing it honestly isn't — shipping it untested would be worse than naming the gap

refutation.rationale: The DECISIONS.md tradeoffs table explicitly names regex-only redaction as a known gap and states that shipping an LLM redaction pass untested 'would be worse than naming the gap.' The claim accurately represents this.

cards.claim: The candidate cites a specific law requiring employers to disclose AI use in hiring — Ontario's Working for Workers Four Act, 2024 — and names the date it takes effect.

citation.quote:
Ontario's *Working
  for Workers Four Act, 2024* requires employers with 25+ employees to
  disclose AI use in screening, assessment, or selection in publicly
  advertised job postings as of January 1, 2026.

refutation.rationale: The README quotes the Ontario law by full name, describes its requirement, and gives the January 1, 2026 effective date. The claim matches the text exactly.

cards.claim: The candidate presents a cut list with explicit reasons for each omission — including auth, database persistence, and video ingestion — and separates 'not now' items from things that will never be built and why.

citation.quote:
| Now | Not now (named next steps) | Never (design decisions) |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence board, skeptic pass, probe gate, decision log, transparency page | LLM redaction pass (regex ships; prose style can still proxy demographics — named risk) | Scores, rankings, pass/fail — no field for them exists |

refutation.rationale: The cut list table does show Now / Not now / Never columns, but the claim specifically mentions 'auth, database persistence, and video ingestion' with explicit reasons. Auth and video ingestion appear in the 'Not now' column without detailed reasons in that table; the reasons are spread elsewhere in the document. The claim slightly overstates the table's own content by saying reasons are given for each omission within the cut list itself.

cards.claim: The candidate leads their risk register with the risk they concede rather than defend — that the tool shapes reviewer decisions just by choosing which evidence to surface — and explicitly states it is not neutral.

citation.quote:
**Evidence selection is itself decision-shaping.** Choosing which twelve
   claims a reviewer sees shapes the review even when humans hold every
   verdict. I claim auditability — every selection is logged, citable, and
   challengeable — not neutrality. No such tool is neutral; distrust any that
   claims to be.

refutation.rationale: The risk register in DECISIONS.md opens with 'Evidence selection is itself decision-shaping' and explicitly states 'I claim auditability… not neutrality.' The claim that this is the first and conceded risk is directly supported.

cards.claim: The candidate names automation bias as a real risk, describes two mitigations built into the product, and honestly says neither has been tested with real users yet.

citation.quote:
**Automation bias.** Reviewers may confirm-click through AI cards.
   Mitigations built: the probe gate forces card-by-card engagement before any
   summary is visible; the override-rate chip makes rubber-stamping visible.
   Honest answer: this needs testing with real panelists, and that test is the
   first thing I'd run with more time.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md names automation bias, lists two specific mitigations (probe gate and override-rate chip), and honestly says 'this needs testing with real panelists.' The claim matches the text accurately.

cards.claim: The candidate is explicit about what the synthetic test data can and cannot prove — it validates the mechanism but not extraction quality at scale — and every number in the eval report carries a label saying it is illustrative.

citation.quote:
Synthetic fixtures are a fair test of mechanism. They cannot validate
  extraction quality at scale — and nothing here claims they do.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md states 'Synthetic fixtures are a fair test of mechanism. They cannot validate extraction quality at scale — and nothing here claims they do.' The README also says every eval number carries an 'illustrative — synthetic fixtures' label. Both parts of the claim are backed.

probes.gap: The pipeline table labels each stage's autonomy level but the skeptic's review found no clear explanation of why each level was chosen — only the labels themselves.
probes.question: Your pipeline table shows three different levels of AI control — 'create-only,' 'annotate-only,' and 'constrained.' Can you walk me through why you picked each one? What would have gone wrong if you'd given the AI more control at any of those stages?

probes.gap: The eval suite and CI configuration are described in the write-up but the actual report and CI config files were not included in the submission, so the claim that CI fails on violations cannot be confirmed.
probes.question: You say the build fails automatically if an eval check breaks. Can you show us the CI config or a recent build log where that actually happened? Walk us through what a failing run looks like.

probes.gap: The cut list table is marked 'unverified' because the reasons for specific omissions like auth and video ingestion are not in the table itself — they appear elsewhere in the document, so it's unclear how readily a reader could find them.
probes.question: Your cut list mentions things like auth and video ingestion as 'not now.' Where in the submission does someone find the reason each of those was left out? Can you give me the reasoning for one of them right now?

probes.gap: The live demo runs on pre-computed outputs by default. It's not clear how much of the real pipeline a reviewer can actually observe, and whether the 'Re-run pipeline' button works reliably end to end.
probes.question: The demo runs on pre-saved results by default, but there's a button to run the real pipeline. Can you walk us through what happens when someone clicks that — what runs, where it could fail, and how a user would know if something went wrong?

probes.gap: Card ev-13 carries a 'citation-mismatch' flag, meaning the source of the quote may not match where it was attributed. The substance of the failure story is supported, but the flag raises a question about accuracy.
probes.question: You describe a specific bug where your injection-resistance check was passing when it shouldn't have been. Which file or document does that account come from, and can you point us to the exact section?

probes.gap: Card ev-15 also carries a 'citation-mismatch' flag on the recall metric story. Same concern — the account is credible but the sourcing needs checking.
probes.question: You explain that you changed how recall was measured because the original definition was unstable. Can you tell us where that's written up, and walk us through what the old check looked like versus the new one?

probes.gap: The reusability claim — that swapping one config file lets the pipeline work for vendor proposals or policy review — is described but not demonstrated. There's no artifact showing it working for any use case other than hiring review.
probes.question: You say someone could reuse this for reviewing vendor proposals just by swapping the rubric file. Have you actually tried that? If so, what broke or needed more than just the file swap?

probes.gap: The candidate names prose style as a gap in the redaction approach but says an AI-based fix was not shipped because it wasn't tested. It's not clear what a good test of that fix would look like or how close it is to being ready.
probes.question: You flagged that even after redaction, writing style could still hint at someone's background, and you held back the AI fix because you hadn't tested it honestly. What would that honest test look like? What would you need to be confident enough to ship it?

probes.gap: The automation bias risk is named and two mitigations are described, but the candidate says neither has been tested with real users. It's worth understanding how the candidate would design that test.
probes.question: You're honest that the automation bias mitigations haven't been tested with real users. If you had a week and a small group of actual hiring reviewers, how would you run that test? What would a bad result look like?

probes.gap: The five criteria for 'evaluate well' are clearly stated, but it's not clear how the candidate arrived at those five — whether they came from research, stakeholder input, or personal judgment.
probes.question: You defined five criteria for what it means to evaluate a candidate well. How did you land on those five? Did you consider other criteria and cut them, or did these come straight out of the brief?

paragraphs.text: The evidence for problem framing (C1) is consistently supported. The candidate clearly explains why they chose not to build a scoring tool, ties that choice to a named governance policy from the hiring organisation, and defines five concrete criteria for what 'evaluate well' means in this context. All four C1 cards are graded 'described' and all are marked supported by the skeptic. The reasoning is credible and clearly written, though it lives in the documents rather than in a runnable artifact.

The workflow design (C2) is the strongest area in terms of artifact evidence. The five-stage pipeline table, the hard lock on the probe sheet until a human reviews every card, and the annotate-only skeptic stage are all directly visible in the submission and confirmed by the skeptic. The one open question is whether the choice of autonomy level at each stage is explained beyond the label — the skeptic found the 'why' for each level thin, and the interview probe on this point is high priority.

Builder execution (C3) is well evidenced for the core tool: a live demo exists, the no-score rule is enforced in code via schema validation rather than a prompt instruction, and specific files are named. The skeptic confirmed all three. The reuse claim — that swapping one config file adapts the pipeline to other domains — is described but not shown working, and the demo runs on pre-computed outputs by default, so the live pipeline path is less directly observable.

Evaluation discipline (C4) and responsible AI (C5) both show a mix of strong and thin evidence. On evals, the candidate reports specific precision numbers, names a real failure in the injection-resistance check, and explains two iterations on the recall metric — all confirmed by the skeptic. However, the actual eval report and CI configuration were not in the submitted documents, so the claim that CI fails on violations is unverified. Two cards in this area also carry citation-mismatch flags, worth checking before the interview. On responsible AI, the transparency page, injection handling, and bias disclosure are all demonstrated and confirmed; the main open item is the untested redaction gap and the untested automation bias mitigations, both of which the candidate names honestly. Communication of tradeoffs (C6) is well supported: the candidate leads with a conceded risk, names automation bias with honest limits, and distinguishes what the synthetic test data can and cannot prove.

Extracted 23 evidence cards. Every card starts unconfirmed; only a human can change that.
Skeptic verdicts attached: 3 of 23 cards contested (unverified or contradicted). Disagreements are surfaced, not resolved.
Drafted 10 interview probes and a 4-paragraph synthesis (locked until every cited card is dispositioned by a human).
